source_text: At hoc in contrarium torqueri potest, ut dicatur: Sed malo aptata natura est; nam quia malum voluntarium esse non poterat, si necessitas fuisset mali, ob hoc data est possibilitas boni, ut malo proprietas pararetur. Quod quidem acutum est, sed insanum; omnia enim rerum a meliore parte taxantur: huc et dignitas auctoris accedit, id est, Dei, qui non ob ea quae puniturus erat, liberum animal fecit; sed propter ea qua remuneraturus, possibilitatem contrariorum dedit. Verumtamen super hoc pugnare nolo; sed permitto aliquid calumniae, ut nihil de opificis auctoritate praescribam. Illud tamen necessario sequitur, ut haec possibilitas faciendi boni et mali removeatur ab utriusque voluntatis effectu. Ac per hoc, nec virtutis a necessario probatur causa esse, nec vitii. Ut enim honestis hanc faciamus iniuriam, ut ex eo quo cum improbis certare videantur, nec bonae ei, nec malae adscribatur meritum voluntatis; habet ergo testimonium ingenuitatis suae, quod innocens est, quia nec bono, nec malo, voluntario dumtaxat, plena est. Possibilitatem ergo voluntatis adscribe naturae; voluntatem autem nec bonam, nec malam, naturae. Invicte ergo collectum est, voluntatem malam exortam quidem in opere Dei; sed a possibili, non a necessario; quod reputari non potest possibilitatis datori, sed possibilitatis ipsius gubernatori.
pass_a_gloss: But this can be twisted into the contrary, so that it is said: But nature was fitted for evil; for because evil could not be voluntary, if there had been a necessity of evil, on account of this a possibility of good was given, that a property might be prepared for evil. Which indeed is acute, but insane; for all things are assessed from the better part: hither also the dignity of the author accedes, that is of God, who did not make a free animal on account of those things which he was about to punish; but on account of those things by which he was about to reward, he gave a possibility of contraries. Nevertheless I do not want to fight upon this; but I permit something of calumny, that I may prescribe nothing from the craftsman's authority. That nevertheless necessarily follows, that this possibility of doing good and evil is removed from the effect of each will. And through this it is proved the cause neither of virtue from the necessary, nor of vice. For that we may do this injury to the honorable, that from that by which they seem to contend with the wicked, the desert of will is ascribed to it neither good nor evil; it has therefore a testimony of its freeborn-ness, that it is innocent, because it is full of neither good nor evil, of the voluntary at least. Ascribe therefore the possibility of will to nature; but will neither good nor evil to nature. It has therefore been unconquerably gathered that an evil will arose indeed in a work of God; but from the possible, not from the necessary; which cannot be credited to the giver of possibility, but to the governor of possibility itself.

pass_b_english: But this can be twisted in the opposite direction: ‘Nature was suited for evil. Since evil could not be voluntary if evil were necessary, the possibility of good was given so that evil could belong to the person as his own.’ This is indeed clever, but insane. Everything is assessed from its better side. Added to this is the dignity of its maker, God: he did not make a free living being for the things he would punish, but gave the possibility of opposites for the things he would reward. Nevertheless, I do not want to fight over this. I allow something to the false objection by declining to settle anything through the maker’s authority. What necessarily follows, however, is that this capacity to do good and evil must be distinguished from the actual result of either will. It is consequently proved to be the necessary cause of neither virtue nor vice.

Even if we insult honorable things by treating their contest with the wicked as grounds to attribute to this capacity neither the merit of a good will nor that of an evil one, it retains the testimony of its freedom: it is innocent because it is full of neither good nor evil—that is, voluntary good or evil. Attribute the possibility of will to nature, then, but attribute neither good nor evil will to nature. The invincible conclusion is that an evil will indeed arose in God’s work, but from possibility, not necessity. This cannot be imputed to the giver of the capacity, but to the one directing that capacity.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
